name: Windows Misc (registry/accounts/wsl)
description: Protects against destructive Windows cmd operations: `reg delete`, \ `net user|localgroup /delete`, `sc delete`, `schtasks /delete`, \ `wsl --unregister` (destroys a WSL distro), and `robocopy /MIR` (mirror \ delete).

destructive_patterns.name: reg-delete
destructive_patterns.description: reg delete removes registry keys/values, which can break apps or Windows.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`reg delete <key>` removes a registry key and all of its values and subkeys; with `/f` \ it does so without confirmation. The registry holds app and OS configuration, so a \ wrong key can break software, services, or the boot path, and there is no Recycle Bin \ for the registry.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - reg export <key> backup.reg: back up the key first (undo with `reg import`) \ - reg query <key>: confirm exactly what the key contains before deleting

destructive_patterns.name: net-account-delete
destructive_patterns.description: net user/localgroup /delete removes a user account or local group.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`net user <name> /delete` deletes a local user account (and `net localgroup <name> \ /delete` a group). The account, its group memberships, and access are removed with no \ prompt; the user's profile/data can be orphaned.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - net user <name>: review the account before deleting \ - Disable instead of delete: net user <name> /active:no

destructive_patterns.name: sc-delete
destructive_patterns.description: sc delete removes a Windows service.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`sc delete <service>` permanently removes a Windows service registration. If it is a \ service something depends on, that software stops working until the service is \ reinstalled.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - sc query <service>: confirm the service and its state first \ - sc stop <service> / sc config <service> start= disabled: disable reversibly instead

destructive_patterns.name: schtasks-delete
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`schtasks /delete /tn <task> /f` removes a scheduled task with no prompt; `/tn *` can \ remove many at once. Deleting a task that maintenance, backups, or apps rely on \ silently stops that work from running.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - schtasks /query /tn <task>: confirm the task first \ - schtasks /change /tn <task> /disable: disable reversibly instead of deleting

destructive_patterns.name: wsl-unregister
destructive_patterns.description: wsl --unregister irreversibly destroys a WSL distribution and its filesystem.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`wsl --unregister <distro>` deregisters a WSL distribution and DELETES its entire \ filesystem — every file, package, and change inside that Linux environment is gone with \ no undo. It is a frequent footgun when a reset/restart was intended.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - wsl --export <distro> backup.tar: back up the whole distro first \ - wsl --terminate <distro>: stop it without destroying it

destructive_patterns.name: robocopy-mirror
destructive_patterns.description: robocopy /MIR deletes destination files that are not present in the source.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`robocopy <src> <dst> /MIR` (mirror) and `/PURGE` delete files and directories in the \ DESTINATION that do not exist in the source — the Windows equivalent of `rsync \ --delete`. A wrong destination, or a source that is missing/empty, wipes the \ destination's contents.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - robocopy <src> <dst> /E: copy subdirectories WITHOUT deleting extras \ - Add /L to /MIR first: list what WOULD change without touching anything
